book_title: The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil
subject_line: The old seaside house in The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil
email_body:
Dear Shubnum,

I was struck by how The Lost Love of Akbar Manzil grows out of Durban itself: you've described the city's coast as full of strange, grand houses that have aged into dilapidation, rather than one house you modelled the mansion on.

I'd love to ask how, over roughly eight years of writing, the love story you set out to tell became a whole life story.

subject_line: The years 2016 to 2018 in The Comrade's Wife
email_body:
Dear Barbara,

The Comrade's Wife caught my attention for its timing: a novel set between 2016 and 2018 that follows rising class status and the promises of transformation and democracy - what you called, at its UCT Writers Series launch, a romance with plots and subplots.

I'd be curious how you balance the romance with the political story, and how your work on Black South African women's novels feeds into your fiction.

email_body:
Beste Bibi

Dit is opvallend dat 'n debuutbundel met die titel Fotostaatmasjien die Eugène Marais-prys, die UJ-prys, die Elisabeth Eybers-prys en die ATKV-Woordveertjie gewen het. 'n Kopieermasjien as titelbeeld vir oorspronklike gedigte bly 'n interessante keuse.

Ek wil graag vra waarom jy daardie beeld gekies het, en hoe jou werk as joernalis en jou meestersgraad in kreatiewe skryfwerk aan Stellenbosch die bundel gevorm het.

The Author Ledger is 'n onafhanklike projek met kort skrywersportrette. Die portret word opgebou uit 'n paar geskrewe vrae wat jy op jou eie tyd kan beantwoord, en die volledige teks word aan jou gestuur om na te gaan voordat dit gepubliseer word.

Sou jy kans sien om deel te neem? Geen druk nie.

Vriendelike groete
The Author Ledger
hook_note: Debut Fotostaatmasjien (Tafelberg 2016) won Eugène Marais, UJ, Elisabeth Eybers and ATKV Woordveertjie prizes; poet/journalist with Stellenbosch MA in Creative Writing (ESAT, LitNet). Later collection Soekenjin (2023). City = Stellenbosch study tie, residence unverified.

subject_line: Waarom 'n mens nie hierdie boek moet eet nie
email_body:
Beste Jaco

subject_line: Thirty readings of Coetzee before Michael K
email_body:

I came across your Business Day interview about Michael K, where you said you had read Coetzee's Life and Times of Michael K around thirty times, yet still mainly wanted to write a good story. Taking up someone else's famous character feels like a risky way to make something your own.

I'd like to ask how you found Michael K's voice apart from Coetzee's, and whether that experience shaped later books such as BREASTS, etc.

subject_line: Is Ōkiwi Brown really William Hare?
email_body:
Dear Cristina,

Ōkiwi Brown takes a real figure who kept a hostelry at Rona Bay and lets the Edinburgh body-snatching case drift into early Port Nicholson. I liked that the book never fully settles whether the whaler on the eastern shore is William Hare.

I'd like to ask how you decided where the historical record ended and invention began, and why you chose to leave that identity question open.

subject_line: Two Ngāpuhi women warriors in A Book of Rongo and Te Rangahau
email_body:
Dear Briar,

A Book of Rongo and Te Rangahau caught my attention for the way it reimagines two nineteenth-century Ngāpuhi women warriors alongside poems about Te Tai Tokerau today. After Rāwāhi travelled out to London and Europe and back, this book seems to stay close to home.

I'd like to ask how you came to Rongo and Te Rangahau, and how living in Whangārei shapes the way you write their stories.
